subjective.question: Define systematics.
subjective.answer: According to Simpson (1961), systematics is the scientific study of the kinds and diversity of organisms and of any or all relationships among them. It is a broad term which includes taxonomy, nomenclature and classification.

subjective.question: What are the components (component fields) of systematics?
subjective.answer: The component fields of systematics are: Biodiversity, Taxonomy, Classification, Nomenclature, Biogeography and Evolutionary biology.

subjective.question: Write a short note on the history of taxonomy.
subjective.answer: Simpson in 1961 gave a valuable survey of the history of taxonomy. Taxonomy is as old as the language skill of mankind. Taxonomy is the science of naming, describing and classifying organisms, including all plants, animals and microorganisms of the world.

subjective.question: What is theoretical biology?
subjective.answer: Theoretical biology is a subdiscipline of biology which employs theoretical analysis, mathematical models and abstractions of living organisms to investigate the principles that govern the structure, development and behaviour of systems, as opposed to experimental biology which deals with the conduction of experiments. Its meaning for the biological sciences is comparable to the meaning of theoretical physics for the physical sciences. It includes evolution, ecology, molecular biology and evolutionary biology.

subjective.question: What is a catalogue? What is the Catalogue of Life?
subjective.answer: A catalogue is mainly an index to the taxa, arranged in such a way as to give a vivid picture of references for both zoological and nomenclatural purposes. The Catalogue of Life is an online database that provides the most comprehensive and authoritative index of known species of organisms on Earth. Its interface is available in twelve languages and is used by research scientists, citizen scientists, educators and policy makers.

subjective.question: What are taxonomic keys? Describe their use in identification.
subjective.answer: A taxonomic key is a simple tool used to identify a specific object. It is one of the most useful tools available to scientists trying to identify an unknown organism. Systematists rely on keys to help identify known organisms and to determine whether they have discovered an entirely new organism.

subjective.question: What is weighing (weighting) of characters? Name its types.
subjective.answer: The process used to determine which character is more reliable is called weighting (weighing of characters). It is of two types: (1) A priori weighting, proposed by Aristotle, done before/without phyletic information; (2) A posteriori weighting, proposed by Adanson, done after phyletic information has been collected. All classification is based on the a posteriori model.

subjective.question: What are correlated characters? Why do they carry low weight in classification?
subjective.answer: Characters which are functionally correlated have very low weight: they have low phylogenetic content and do not deserve to be treated as separate characters. Analogous organs (e.g. wings of birds, bats and insects) are the result of convergent evolution and are redundant. Phyletic correlation, on the other hand, has high weight and higher genetic content, e.g. the diagnostic characters of Deuterostomes and Chordates (concordance).

subjective.question: What are morphological characters? List their main types.
subjective.answer: Morphology describes the structural features of animals. Morphological characters include: external morphology, genetic structure, internal morphology, embryology, and karyology and other cytological differences.

subjective.question: What are physiological characters? Give examples.
subjective.answer: Physiological characters include: metabolic activities, body secretions, serological (protein) and other biochemical differences, and the genic sterility factor.

subjective.question: What are the causes of speciation?
subjective.answer: The main causes of speciation are: (1) Geographical isolation, (2) Behavioural isolation, and (3) Reproductive isolation.

subjective.question: Define sympatric speciation.
subjective.answer: Sympatric speciation is a speciation in which a new species is evolved from a single common ancestral species while inhabiting the same geographical range. The populations share the same habitat but become reproductively isolated from each other. It is more common in plants.

subjective.question: Define peripatric speciation.
subjective.answer: Peripatric speciation is a mode of speciation in which a new species is formed from an isolated peripheral population.

subjective.question: Define an evolutionary species.
subjective.answer: Simpson (1940s) defined an evolutionary species, later stated by Wiley (1981), as a single lineage of ancestor-descendant populations of organisms which maintains its identity from other such lineages in space and time, and which has its own evolutionary tendencies and historical fate.

subjective.question: What is the biological species concept? Write its main criticisms.
subjective.answer: The biological species concept defines a species as groups of actually or potentially interbreeding natural populations which are reproductively isolated from other such groups. Its main criticisms/limitations are that it is not applicable on asexually reproducing individuals and not applicable on sibling/cryptic species; the concept centres on interbreeding natural populations, while incomplete speciation is not counted among these criticisms.

subjective.question: Differentiate between gynandromorphs and intersexes.
subjective.answer: Gynandromorphs are individuals that show male characters in one part of the body and female characters in other parts, i.e. the two sexes are present in separate body regions (a mosaic). Intersexes, on the other hand, show a blending of male and female characters throughout the body rather than in separate parts.

subjective.question: What are ecological variations? List their types.
subjective.answer: Ecological variations include: A. Habitat variation, B. Variations induced by climatic conditions, C. Host-determined variations, D. Density-dependent variations, E. Allometric variations, and F. Neurogenic colour variations.

subjective.question: What are postmortem variations? Explain briefly.
subjective.answer: Postmortem changes begin soon after death and progress along a timeline. Two processes, putrefaction and autolysis, begin to alter the body; either one may predominate depending on the circumstances surrounding death and the climate. Putrefaction involves the action of bacteria on the tissues of the body. In collections, it is impossible to prevent post-mortem changes in some animals; for example, the Chinese jay's plumage changes from green to blue in collection.

subjective.question: What are traumatic variations? Define teratology and teratogens.
subjective.answer: Teratology is the study of abnormalities of physical development. Teratogens are the toxic substances which cause abnormal development, e.g. mercury, alcohol, lead and thalidomide. Teratological (traumatic) variations are common in animals; in forms which undergo metamorphosis, injury to an earlier stage may produce abnormalities which are not easily recognized. They are important if the abnormality is in characters of taxonomic importance, e.g. modification in wing pattern.

subjective.question: Define random sampling.
subjective.answer: If every individual of the target population has an equal chance of selection, it is called random sampling. Simple random sampling is the easiest form of probability sampling; no bias and no expert opinion is required in this method.

subjective.question: Describe the types of probability sampling.
subjective.answer: Probability sampling includes: (1) Random sampling — every individual has an equal chance of selection. (2) Systematic sampling — the first sample is taken randomly and afterwards samples are selected systematically at regular intervals. (3) Stratified sampling — the population is divided into different subgroups or strata and subjects are randomly selected proportionally from the different strata. (4) Cluster sampling — different groups within a population are used as the sample. (5) Multistage sampling — the population is split into smaller and smaller groups and samples are taken from the smallest resulting groups. Types of systematic sampling are: systematic random sampling, linear systematic sampling and circular systematic sampling.

subjective.question: How does systematics contribute to applied biology? Explain with examples.
subjective.answer: Systematics contributes to applied biology in: agriculture and forestry, biological control, public health, quarantine, wildlife management, mineral prospecting, national defense, environmental problems, soil fertility and commerce. In agriculture and forestry, correct names and identification of pests are necessary to control and minimize pest attack on crops and vector-borne diseases; taxonomists give the correct identification of pests, which is vital for control and for designing biological control programs (e.g. the parasitic wasp Tamarixia radiata, introduced from Pakistan to California against the Asian citrus psyllid — a classic example of biological control). In public health, many diseases are spread by arthropods and are controlled by targeting the specific species involved; for example, not all Anopheles maculipennis are responsible for transmitting malaria, and taxonomists identify the particular sibling species for effective control at minimum cost. In wildlife management, it helps environmental protectors by identifying economically and ecologically important wildlife.

subjective.question: Describe the arthropod venom glands and their parts.
subjective.answer: Venoms serve two primary roles — defense and prey capture. The arthropod venom (poison) apparatus consists of three parts: (1) Poison gland, (2) Poison duct, and (3) Fang.

subjective.question: Name the parts of an arthropod leg in order.
subjective.answer: The parts of an arthropod leg are: Coxa, Trochanter, Femur, Patella, Tibia, Metatarsus, Tarsus and Claws.

subjective.question: Describe the jumping behaviour of jumping spiders.
subjective.answer: Jumping spiders are generally diurnal, active hunters. They have a well-developed internal hydraulic system: they extend their limbs by altering the pressure of their body fluid (hemolymph) within them. This enables the spider to jump without having large muscular legs like a grasshopper.

subjective.question: Describe the feeding process of jumping spiders.
subjective.answer: Jumping spiders are mostly carnivorous. They eat insects like flies, moths and grasshoppers. They are predominantly carnivores, though they have been known to eat nectar as well. In general, jumping spiders eat anything they can get their chelicerae (jaws) around.

subjective.question: How can a jumping spider be identified?
subjective.answer: A jumping spider can be identified by: colour (black or brown, tan or gray, usually with pale markings), legs (four pairs of legs, relatively short), shape, absence of antennae, and its region (e.g. found in the United States).

subjective.question: Describe reproduction in spiders.
subjective.answer: In spiders, the male first finds a female. A male spider deposits his sperm into a sperm web and holds it in his palps, from which it is transferred to the female. Female spiders produce either one egg sac containing several to a thousand eggs, or several egg sacs each with successively fewer eggs. Females of many species die after producing the last egg sac.

subjective.question: Describe the courtship behaviour in the lynx spider.
subjective.answer: In a typical mating sequence of the green lynx spider, courtship lasted about 11 minutes. Mating took about 10 minutes, consisting of several copulations measured from the first approach of a male palpus to the female's epigynum until the final separation.

subjective.question: Describe variations in insects with reference to their life cycles.
subjective.answer: One way in which insects can differ is by the type of life cycles they have. Some insects undergo incomplete metamorphosis and change from a nymph to an adult. Others go through complete metamorphosis with many stages: they start as larvae, which look very different from adults, and when they emerge from their pupa they are newly formed adults.

subjective.question: What is DNA hybridization? What is it used for?
subjective.answer: DNA hybridization is a method used to determine the genetic distance between two organisms; it mainly measures their genetic similarity.

subjective.question: Name some methods of collecting specimens. How are the collected samples preserved?
subjective.answer: Specimens are collected by different methods according to the animal group: sweep nets are used to collect arthropods from grass, an aspirator is used to collect small insects, and trawling is a method of fishing used for aquatic collections. The collected samples are then preserved by two methods — the wet method (in preservative fluid) and the dry method — i.e. both of these methods are used according to the nature of the specimen.
